newsitem.title: USA: Record rains bring death, floods to Ohio Valley.
newsitem.headline: Record rains bring death, floods to Ohio Valley.

text.p: Record rains swamped the Ohio Valley, killing at least 10 people in Kentucky and Ohio and forcing evacuations of towns as rivers boiled out of their banks, officials said on Sunday.
West Virginia Gov. Cecil Underwood declared a state of emergency in 15 counties in the southwest of the state where flooding from small streams forced several hundred people from their homes.
The Kentucky Division of Disaster and Emergency Services said eight people drowned in that state and one person was missing. Two deaths were reported in Ohio but eight more people were missing.
The Kentucky Division of Disaster and Emergency Services said eight people died in that state, all by drowning, Two deaths were reported in Ohio but six to eight people were unaccounted for.

In Kentucky, the towns of Falmouth and Butler were devastated by the Licking River which was twice as high as flood stage and had reached rooftop levels. The two towns, home to about 3,500 people, were being evacuated on Sunday.
The Kentucky deaths included a couple whose car was swept off a highway and a 13-year-old boy sucked into a culvert he and his father were trying to clear of debris at the end of their driveway.
In Ohio a couple whose car was swamped by a flash flood on Brush Creek climbed into a tree to escape but one of them, a 34-year-old woman, lost her grip and was swept away.
A 16-year-old boy drowned in a culvert near Blue Creek, Ohio, about 50 miles (80 km) east of Cincinnati.
Thirty-six Kentucky counties and 35 cities declared emergencies. Gov. Paul Patton deployed 200 National Guard troops to help with evacuations and 19 Guard armories were opened as emergency shelters.

Twelve inches (30 cm) of rain fell in Louisville and other parts of Kentucky from late Friday night through Sunday morning. The total included 9.6 inches (24 cm) over a 24-hour period, the most recorded in one day in the city.

The torrential rain caused the Ohio River to rise 19 feet (5.8 metres) in 24 hours to a flood stage of 52 feet (15.8 metres) in Cincinnati on Sunday. The U.S. Weather Service said the river would crest at more than 61 feet (18.6 metres) on Wednesday, the highest level since 1964.

Riverfront restaurants in Covington, Kentucky across the river from Cincinnati were closed, one small village near Cincinnati was evacuated and River Downs race track in the area was shut after roads leading into it were flooded.
About five inches (12 cm) of rain fell in parts of southern Ohio.

An interstate highway in Louisville was closed for a time and parts of other interstates in the state remained closed on Sunday, along with many other streets and secondary highways. Frankfort, the state capital, was hit by flooding along the Kentucky River described as the worst there in 20 years.
Three state office buildings in Frankfort were ordered closed on Monday.
A 142-year-old covered bridge, one of 14 such historic structures remaining in Kentucky, was torn from its foundation and destroyed on Elkhorn Creek, a tributary of the Kentucky River near Frankfort.
Paris, Kentucky, in the bluegrass horse breeding area near Lexington was without power, telephones or sewer service because of flooding on Stoner Creek, a tributary of the Licking.
